issues.legal_issue: An administrative direction to displace existing allottees is a final cancellation order when its language and context show that displacement has been decided, even if immediate implementation is deferred.
material_facts: The administrative order stated that the existing allottees would have to move out to make room for other allottees, referred to them as persons to be ousted, and directed that alternative land be sought for them.
The order indicated that immediate action would await the outcome of a pending appeal; the court read the qualification as postponing the timing of displacement, not making the decision tentative.
The challengers had sought to have the order quashed as a cancellation order and later argued that it was only a proposal.
issues.conclusion: The order was a final decision to cancel the allotments, not a mere proposal or tentative order; the challengers could not advance a position contrary to the one taken in their writ petition.
issues.legal_principle: An administrative order is construed from its language and context. A statement postponing immediate action does not make an otherwise decided action tentative. A litigant may not be permitted to advance a contention clearly contrary to the position taken in that litigant’s own pleading. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_an_administrative_: The proceeding challenges an administrative decision affecting an existing allotment.
predicates.order_directs_displacement: The administrative order directs the affected allottees to leave so that others can be accommodated.
predicates.order_defers_only_immediate_execution: The order postpones immediate action without making the underlying decision conditional or tentative.
predicates.challengers_sought_quashing_as_a_final_o: The challengers initially sought to quash the order on the basis that it was a final decision affecting them.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges an administrative cancellation, the order directs displacement, only immediate execution is deferred, and the challengers sought to quash it as final, the order is treated as a final cancellation.

issues.legal_issue: A saved administrative order that was not implemented by an earlier cutoff may be implemented after a later amendment removes the restriction on its implementation.
material_facts: The action against the allottees was taken under rules contained in an earlier government notification.
A later rule-making notification repealed those rules and initially provided that certain orders would have no effect if not implemented by a specified cutoff.
That restriction was deleted by a subsequent amendment before the court considered whether the order could be implemented.
issues.conclusion: The failure to implement the order by the former cutoff did not prohibit its implementation after the restriction was deleted.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 49 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950 saved actions taken under the repealed rules, subject initially to a proviso restricting the effect of certain unimplemented orders. The amendment of August 4, 1952 deleted that proviso; the court held that non-implementation by the former cutoff therefore no longer barred later implementation. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_late_implementatio: The proceeding challenges the later implementation of an earlier administrative order.
predicates.order_was_made_under_repealed_rules: The administrative order was made under rules that were subsequently repealed, with actions under them saved by the replacement rules.
predicates.order_was_not_implemented_by_former_cuto: The order had not been implemented by the cutoff that previously applied to it.
predicates.later_amendment_removed_implementation_r: A later amendment removed the restriction that had barred implementation after the cutoff.

issues.definition: If a proceeding challenges late implementation of a saved order that missed the former cutoff, and a later amendment removes the implementation restriction, the order may be implemented later.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising constitutional writ jurisdiction may review its own order to prevent miscarriage of justice or correct grave and palpable errors, including where the earlier order affected persons who were not heard.
material_facts: An earlier writ order affected the interests of persons who had not been made parties to the proceeding.
Those persons applied to the High Court to be impleaded and to have the matter reheard so that they could be heard.
The High Court entertained the application and reheard the matter.
issues.conclusion: Article 226 did not preclude the High Court from exercising its inherent review power, and the High Court could entertain the affected persons’ application to give them a hearing.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 does not prevent a High Court from exercising the review power inherent in a court of plenary jurisdiction to prevent miscarriage of justice or correct grave and palpable errors. The principles of natural justice support hearing persons whose interests are affected by an order made without their participation. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.proceeding_is_under_constitutional_writ_: The matter arises in a proceeding in which the High Court exercises constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.prior_order_affected_absent_persons: An earlier order affected the interests of persons who were not parties to the proceeding in which it was made.
predicates.affected_persons_seek_a_hearing: The persons whose interests were affected apply to be heard and seek reconsideration of the earlier order.

issues.definition: When a writ order affects persons who were not heard and they seek a hearing, the High Court may review its order.
